blocks.text: A **computer network** links digital devices so they can exchange data and share resources such as files, applications, storage, Internet access and printers. One office printer, for example, can serve many connected computers.

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: Any device or connection point taking part in a network: computer, server, printer, router or switch.
These are **roles** a node plays, not types of network participants. Every participant is a node.
A set of communication rules covering message format, transmission and handling.
A way of splitting communication into tasks so networks are easier to design and troubleshoot.

blocks.title: Early networking milestones
items: **ARPANET** (Advanced Research Projects Agency Network) becomes operational, funded through ARPA of the US Department of Defense.
**TCP/IP** is developed; Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn are its leading designers.
ARPANET switches from **NCP** (Network Control Protocol) to **TCP/IP**.
ISO publishes the first Basic Reference Model standard for **OSI**.

blocks.text: ARPANET pioneered **packet switching** and helped lead to the Internet, but it was not the first network of every kind. The Internet had many contributors, so Cerf and Kahn are called leading developers rather than sole inventors.

blocks.title: Quick recall
blocks.text: ARPANET 1969 | TCP/IP transition 1983 | OSI standard 1984.

**OSI** (Open Systems Interconnection) is a seven-layer reference model. It is a conceptual framework, not one program, but real networks can be described using its layers. Read it from layer 7 down to layer 1.

blocks.title: The seven OSI layers (top to bottom)
items: 7 Application
Network services used by applications
6 Presentation
Data format, compression, encryption-related
5 Session
Starts, manages and closes sessions
4 Transport
End-to-end delivery, ports, TCP/UDP
3 Network
Logical (IP) addressing and routing
2 Data Link
Local delivery, framing, MAC addresses
1 Physical
Raw bits as electrical, optical or radio signals

blocks.title: Layer details
rows: Data representation, format conversion, compression and encryption-related functions
Process-to-process (end-to-end) transfer; segmentation and reassembly; port numbers
Local-link delivery, framing, MAC addressing, frame error detection (FCS)
Bridges, ordinary Ethernet switches, MAC address
Transmits bits as electrical, optical or radio signals
Hubs, repeaters, cables, basic modem signal conversion

blocks.title: Abbreviations
rows: Protocol Data Unit: the name of the data chunk at a layer.
Frame Check Sequence: used at the Data Link layer to detect frame errors.

blocks.title: Encapsulation going down the stack
items: Data
From the upper layers
TCP segment
Transport adds ports (UDP makes a datagram)
IP packet
Network adds IP addresses
Frame
Data Link adds MAC addresses and FCS
Bits
Physical sends signals

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.text: Top to bottom: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. Addresses: Layer 4 = ports, Layer 3 = IP, Layer 2 = MAC. Going upward: bits, frames, packets, segments, data.

blocks.title: Things to be careful about
items: Layers 5-7 are commonly called the **upper layers**; Layer 4 connects application communication with network delivery.
Hardware and software boundaries are not rigid; one device can combine functions across layers.
Error detection and encryption are not exclusive to one layer; their placement depends on the protocol.
A gateway's layers depend on its function. The claim that every gateway works at all seven layers is inaccurate.

blocks.text: **TCP/IP** (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol) is a working protocol suite that grew out of US defence-funded research in the 1970s, with Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn as leading designers. ARPANET adopted it in 1983. It is a large family of Internet protocols, not exactly 100 protocols.

blocks.title: TCP/IP four-layer model (top to bottom)
items: Application
HTTP, DNS, SMTP and other services
Transport / Host-to-Host
TCP and UDP; process-to-process
Internet
IP and ICMP; logical addressing, routing
Network Access / Link
Ethernet, Wi-Fi; local communication

blocks.text: Many books teach a **five-layer model** instead: Application, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical. It simply splits the Link layer into two; it is not a different protocol suite.

blocks.title: No missing layers
blocks.text: TCP/IP has no separate Session or Presentation layer, but those functions are not missing. They are handled inside the TCP/IP Application layer.

blocks.title: Core protocols compared
rows: Reliable, ordered byte stream; uses acknowledgements, retransmissions, flow and congestion control. PDU: segment.
Datagrams with no built-in delivery, ordering or retransmission guarantee; low overhead; no connection-setup handshake.
Packet delivery with no end-to-end reliability guarantee.

blocks.title: UDP wording
blocks.text: UDP has low **overhead** (not 'overload') and needs no handshake. It may reduce delay, but it is not always faster, and it is not inherently reliable.

blocks.title: Transport layer recap
items: Transport = Layer 4 = the **end-to-end layer**: process-to-process communication, segmentation and reassembly, and port numbers.
TCP adds reliability and ordering; end-to-end delivery reliability depends on the chosen transport or application design.
Transport PDU: TCP segment or UDP datagram.

blocks.text: **IEEE** (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) develops technical standards and supports engineering advances for public benefit. The **IEEE 802** family covers local, metropolitan and related area networks.

blocks.title: Standard and what it covers
rows: LAN architecture, bridging, VLANs and higher-layer LAN protocols
Integrated Services LANs, including voice and data
Low-rate wireless Physical and MAC layers used by Zigbee, Thread and others

blocks.title: Quick recall
blocks.text: Ethernet 802.3 | Wi-Fi 802.11 | Bluetooth history 802.15.1 | Zigbee foundation 802.15.4 | WiMAX 802.16. Several entries are historical, withdrawn or tied to disbanded groups, and 802.15.4 is only a foundation for Zigbee, not the whole Zigbee specification.

sections.title: IP addresses: IPv4, IPv6 and classes

blocks.text: An **IP address** (Internet Protocol address) is a logical address given to a network interface. It identifies source and destination and supports routing at OSI Layer 3. Addresses can be static or dynamically assigned, so an IP is not always temporary. Both IPv4 and IPv6 are in use today.

blocks.title: IPv4 vs IPv6
rows: Four decimal octets separated by dots
Eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons
Leading zeros and one run of zeros can be abbreviated

items: The 0-255 range belongs to each IPv4 octet, not to the whole address.
A common IPv6 plan is 48-bit routing prefix + 16-bit subnet ID + 64-bit interface ID, but this is an example and not compulsory.
Plain 'IP address' is ambiguous: say whether IPv4 or IPv6 when the size matters.

blocks.title: Historical classful IPv4
rows: Ordinary unicast range commonly taught as 1-126

blocks.text: Modern networks generally use **CIDR** prefixes instead of classful allocation, so the class system is mostly an exam topic today.

blocks.title: Special addresses
rows: The common loopback address, pointing to the local host.
The whole IPv4 loopback block; it is not ordinary host space.
Limited local broadcast; routers do not forward it.

blocks.text: IPv4 = decimal, 32 bits. IPv6 = hexadecimal, 128 bits.

A **MAC address** (Media Access Control) identifies a network interface for local-link frame delivery at OSI Layer 2, the Data Link layer. A conventional Ethernet MAC has 48 bits = 6 bytes = 12 hexadecimal digits, for example 00:1A:3F:F1:4C:C6. Interfaces (the **NIC**, Network Interface Card) usually carry a manufacturer-assigned address.

blocks.title: Structure of a universally assigned MAC
rows: The **OUI** (Organizationally Unique Identifier), identifying the manufacturer allocation.
Identify the interface within that allocation.

blocks.title: Physical address is not the Physical layer
blocks.text: A MAC is often called a physical or hardware address, but it belongs to Layer 2 (Data Link), not Layer 1 (Physical). Also, a MAC can be overridden or randomized, so 'it never changes' is false.

blocks.title: Address services
rows: Address Resolution Protocol: finds the link-layer (MAC) address for a known IPv4 address on the local link.
Reverse Address Resolution Protocol: legacy, server-assisted discovery of a device's own IP from its hardware address.
Domain Name System: resolves names to records, including IPv4 and IPv6 address records.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: supplies an IP address and settings such as subnet mask, gateway and DNS servers.

items: RARP is legacy; DHCP is the common way to configure hosts.
IP and MAC addresses are addressing concepts, not communication protocols.
Both effective IP and MAC addresses can change.
Recall: ARP = IPv4 to MAC, RARP = reverse, DNS = names, DHCP = configuration.

sections.title: Hubs, repeaters, bridges, switches and routers

blocks.title: Connecting devices
rows: Regenerates and retransmits a signal to extend a link. Does not route using IP.
A multiport repeater: repeats incoming signals to every other port, with no destination-based forwarding or MAC learning. Called a 'dumb device'.
Connects compatible LAN segments; learns MAC addresses and forwards or filters frames. Does not perform general protocol translation.
An ordinary Ethernet switch is a multiport bridge that uses a MAC table to pick the outgoing port. Multilayer switches can also route at Layer 3.
Connects different IP networks and LAN subnets; forwards packets by destination IP and its routing table, choosing a route and next hop.

blocks.title: Router notes
items: Used in LAN and WAN environments; example vendors include Cisco, D-Link and HPE.
Depending on the product, a router may include firewall rules, **VPN** (Virtual Private Network), traffic monitoring and Wi-Fi access.
2.4 GHz and 5 GHz are common Wi-Fi bands, not routing frequencies, and a wired router needs no radio.
A single appliance can combine a modem, router, switch, wireless access point and firewall.

blocks.title: Hub is not a broadcaster
blocks.text: A hub repeats all traffic to every other port, but that is not the same as generating an IP broadcast. It is a Layer 1 device that knows nothing about MAC or IP addresses.

blocks.title: Device memory
blocks.text: Hub or repeater = Layer 1 = bits. Bridge or ordinary switch = Layer 2 = MAC and frames. Router = Layer 3 = IP and packets.

blocks.title: Devices and concepts
rows: An entry and exit point between systems or networks. A **default gateway** is typically the router used to reach other IP networks.
Translates between differing systems or formats; its layers depend on its purpose.
**Mod**ulator-**Dem**odulator. Modulation encodes digital information onto a carrier; demodulation recovers it from the received signal.
Permits or blocks traffic according to security rules. It can be software, an appliance or part of a router, and may inspect addresses, ports, state and application information.

blocks.title: Modem speed
items: Data rate is measured in bits per second (bps), kbps or Mbps.
Baud measures symbols per second and is not always equal to bps.
A 100 Mbps device or link can bottleneck a 500 Mbps service.

blocks.title: Dial-up vs DSL
rows: Faster than dial-up, but fibre can be much faster
Generally always on; voice and data possible with filtering
DSL modem function, sometimes combined with a router

blocks.title: Spoofing
rows: Packets carry a forged source IP address.
False DNS information is accepted, potentially redirecting users.

blocks.text: Changing an IP or DNS setting legitimately is not spoofing. Also, 'every gateway works at all seven layers' is inaccurate, and network size alone does not decide security; configuration and controls do.

sections.title: Email, web, file transfer and remote access

blocks.title: Email protocols
rows: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (not 'Transport'): outgoing mail submission and transfer between mail servers.
Post Office Protocol version 3: downloads messages, commonly for local storage. Server-copy retention depends on settings, and it is not restricted to one device.
Internet Message Access Protocol: accesses mail stored on the server and synchronizes folders and status across devices.
Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions: content formats for attachments, multimedia, non-ASCII text and multipart bodies. It does not send mail by itself.

blocks.title: File transfer, web and remote access
rows: File Transfer Protocol: uploads and downloads between client and server.
SSH File Transfer Protocol (often called Secure File Transfer Protocol): file transfer and management over encrypted SSH. Different from FTP.
Hypertext Transfer Protocol: requests and responses for web resources. The Web is a service running over the Internet.
HTTP over TLS: encrypts and protects communication and authenticates the server. It does not guarantee that site content is trustworthy.
Remote text-terminal access; ordinary Telnet is unencrypted.
Secure Shell: secure remote login, commands and related services.
Legacy protocol for hierarchical menus to distribute and retrieve Internet resources, with search services.
Internet Control Message Protocol: network control, error reports and diagnostics.

blocks.title: Quick recall
blocks.text: SMTP sends | POP3 downloads | IMAP synchronizes | MIME formats content | FTP transfers | SFTP runs over SSH | HTTPS runs over TLS.

blocks.title: Security protocols
rows: Secure **Sockets** Layer (plural): an obsolete protocol family, not a modern strong-security choice.
Transport Layer Security: SSL's successor, providing encryption, integrity and authentication.
Point-to-Point Tunneling Protocol: legacy VPN tunnelling.

blocks.title: Is SMTP a security protocol?
blocks.text: Basic SMTP has no inherent encryption, but TLS can protect it, including through STARTTLS. Old questions that list SSL as secure are outdated, because SSL is obsolete.

blocks.title: Types of port
rows: A connector on equipment, such as an Ethernet socket.
A transport endpoint identifying an application or service. TCP and UDP have separate port spaces numbered 0-65535.

blocks.title: Common service ports
rows: TCP (passive FTP negotiates another server data port)
TCP for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2; UDP for HTTP/3

items: DHCP usually goes client to server 68 to 67, and the reply goes 67 to 68.
These port numbers are conventions; deployments may use other ports.
ICMP, ARP and RARP have no TCP/UDP port numbers, and MIME has no independent transport port.

blocks.title: Port recall
blocks.text: 20/21 FTP | 22 SSH | 23 Telnet | 25 SMTP | 53 DNS | 67/68 DHCP | 80 HTTP | 110 POP3 | 143 IMAP | 443 HTTPS.

A **topology** describes the arrangement of nodes and links. **Physical topology** is the actual connection layout, while **logical topology** is the way communication flows, which may differ from the physical layout.

blocks.title: Topology comparison
rows: Traditional coaxial Ethernet uses terminators at both ends to prevent reflections. Low cable cost, but a backbone failure can disrupt the segment.
Separate link from each endpoint to a central switch (or older hub)
Common Ethernet LAN design. One cable failure usually affects one endpoint; central-device failure affects all attached nodes.
Closed loop, two neighbours per node
Traffic passes around the loop. Token Ring uses a token, but not every ring does. Simple rings need protection against a break.
Often switches linking star-like sections; good for departments or buildings. An upstream failure can cut off lower branches.
Full mesh links every pair; partial mesh links selected pairs. Redundancy improves resilience, but wired full mesh needs many cables and interfaces.
Two or more topology types combined
n(n-1)/2 for one bidirectional link per pair. Six nodes need 6 x 5 / 2 = 15 links.
A direct link between two endpoints.

blocks.title: Exam corrections
blocks.text: 'Mesh is the most reliable' is a simplification; real reliability depends on design. Token passing also occurs in Token Bus, so it is not exclusive to rings. Duplex direction is a property of the link, not of the topology's name.

sections.title: Network types, access and transmission modes

blocks.title: Network types by size
rows: Nearby personal devices such as Bluetooth headphones, keyboard or mouse; infrared links are short range. About 10 m is an example, not a fixed limit.
A limited location such as a home or office; usually privately managed, wired or wireless; shares files and printers. Typical speeds 10 Mbps to 1 Gbps and above.
Interconnected LANs in nearby buildings of an organization (library, hostel, departments, offices). Some texts call it a corporate area network.
City-scale links between sites or LANs, often over fibre. Municipal and cable-TV networks are examples.
Connects distant regions or countries using routers, fibre, leased circuits, cellular, microwave or satellite. The Internet is a global example; satellite is not compulsory.
Specialized network linking servers to shared storage, commonly with block access; used in data centres, arrays and backup. Fibre Channel and iSCSI are examples.

blocks.title: PAN / WLAN distinctions
items: Wireless USB is historically associated with PAN, but a USB Wi-Fi adapter connects to a WLAN.
Wi-Fi hotspots and printers are not automatically PANs.
Two LANs joined together do not automatically make a MAN.

blocks.title: Access types
rows: Global public interconnection; some resources may still be restricted.
A network for authorized internal users.
Selected access for approved partners, customers or suppliers; not only for two companies.

blocks.title: Transmission modes
rows: Broadcast; idealized keyboard input (real keyboards also communicate both ways)
Both ways, one at a time
Both ways at the same time

blocks.text: **Guided media** are physical cables; **unguided media** carry electromagnetic waves through free space. Remember: copper carries electrical signals, fibre carries light, wireless uses electromagnetic waves.

blocks.title: Guided media
rows: Insulated copper wires twisted to reduce interference and crosstalk
UTP (Unshielded) is widely used in Ethernet LANs; STP (Shielded) has metal shielding, helpful in noisy industrial or factory settings but not limited to them
Central conductor, insulation, metal shield and outer jacket
Cable TV and broadband, RF/video, older Ethernet
Light through glass or plastic fibres
High capacity, long distance, immune to electromagnetic interference; broadband, backbones and undersea cables. Actual speed depends on equipment.

blocks.title: Connectors
rows: Registered Jack 45: the common name for twisted-pair Ethernet connectors. The actual Ethernet modular form is 8P8C (eight positions, eight contacts).
Bayonet Neill-Concelman: coaxial connector with bayonet coupling. TV also commonly uses F-type connectors.
Ferrule Connector: fibre, threaded coupling. It is NOT Fibre Channel.

blocks.text: SC, ST and FC commonly use 2.5 mm ferrules, while LC uses 1.25 mm. A ferrule holds and aligns the fibre.

blocks.title: Unguided media
rows: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile and broadcast; coverage depends on frequency, power and environment.
Directional terrestrial or satellite links, often line of sight; technically part of the radio spectrum.
Short-range optical paths, direct or reflected; used by remote controls and device links.

revision: ARPANET went live in 1969; it moved from NCP to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983; the OSI reference standard was published in 1984.
OSI layers top to bottom: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.
PDUs: Data (layers 5-7), segment or datagram (4), packet (3), frame (2), bits (1).
Address memory: Layer 4 = ports, Layer 3 = IP, Layer 2 = MAC.
TCP/IP has no separate Session or Presentation layer; their functions sit in its Application layer.
TCP is connection-oriented and reliable; UDP is connectionless with low overhead and no guarantee; IP is best-effort.
IPv4 = 32 bits (4 decimal octets, each 0-255); IPv6 = 128 bits (hexadecimal groups).
A MAC address is Layer 2: 48 bits = 6 bytes = 12 hex digits; first 24 bits are the OUI.
ARP maps IPv4 to MAC; DHCP supplies IP settings; DNS resolves names; RARP is legacy.
Hub and repeater work at Layer 1, bridge and switch at Layer 2, router at Layer 3.
SMTP sends mail, POP3 downloads it, IMAP synchronizes it; MIME defines content formats.
SSL is obsolete; TLS is its successor; HTTPS is HTTP over TLS; SFTP runs over SSH.
Ports: 20/21 FTP, 22 SSH, 23 Telnet, 25 SMTP, 53 DNS, 67/68 DHCP, 80 HTTP, 110 POP3, 143 IMAP, 443 HTTPS.
Full mesh needs n(n-1)/2 links (6 nodes = 15); bus uses terminators; star uses a central switch.
Duplex modes: simplex one way, half-duplex one at a time, full-duplex both together.
